segment:
Her cheeks warmed and her heart skipped; she wished she could just sit down beside him and touch him. But he was still smiling that gentle smile, looking amused rather than pleased by the idea of her touch.

The room was too big for them both. She swallowed, realizing how awkward it must sound for her to want his name like this—without knowing anything about him. He wasn’t talking anymore either; just staring at her with those green-blue eyes that seemed impossibly open and warm.
There were more people here, though. Other guests in shirts and jeans or shorts stood around talking and laughing near the front door. A woman in a black cocktail dress came through from somewhere else; she recognized Adrian Voss but couldn’t hear what he was saying over all the noise. Then another figure appeared in his wake—a young man carrying an open glass of red wine—and he caught her attention.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

A man, it turned out. Maybe twenty-four or twenty-five? In the same gray cotton T-shirt as the welcome pack that she’d carried in her backpack to the gate, with blue-green eyes and a faint smile that seemed to mean nothing at all. She watched his gaze fall past her head to the entryway, then back.
“Welcome, Mara.”
His voice was low and musical. “Hi.” She tried to steady her breathing, to not look so stiffly out of place. She dropped her pack by the door, then took a slow step inside, hands hanging loose and empty.
“I’m glad you came,” he continued, as though the first words hadn’t been enough.
She waited for him to continue, to introduce himself or say something more; she wanted to know who he was and what he did here. But when he didn’t, she cleared her throat and ventured, “Who are you?”
A faint smile quirked his lips. “That’s not a name,” he said softly.
“What’s yours, then?”
He laughed a little, shaking his head. “Mine?” he asked quietly. “Oh, I guess it depends on what you’d like me to be called.”

The room was too big for them both. She swallowed, realizing how awkward it must sound for her to want his name like this—without knowing anything about him. He wasn’t talking anymore either; just staring at her with those green-blue eyes that seemed impossibly open and warm.
There were more people here, though. Other guests in shirts and jeans or shorts stood around talking and laughing near the front door. A woman in a black cocktail dress came through from somewhere else; she recognized Adrian Voss but couldn’t hear what he was saying over all the noise. Then another figure appeared in his wake—a young man carrying an open glass of red wine—and he caught her attention.

segment:
This seemed like a joke; she wasn’t sure how to respond. But the room was full of sounds other than their voices now, and there were other people in the doorway. Men and women, talking amongst themselves but clearly coming to join them here; one young fellow carried a glass. The door closed softly behind them as Mara turned to face it.
A woman—a woman who’d already said something about Mara’s backpack—was looking at her with wide eyes. She was pretty in an ordinary way, short dark hair framing her face and a soft voice that seemed to catch the edges of the room with each word she spoke. Mara’s heart raced as they drew closer; she felt like she could see herself reflected on those pale cheeks, see the young woman looking at her own reflection for the first time.
“I’m so glad you came,” the woman said brightly. “Welcome home.”

segment:
She swallowed against the sensation that she was already being taken advantage of, and tried again. “Your name. What’s your first name?”
His eyes narrowed slightly; they were a deeper green than she’d thought, darker than emerald or jade. She waited as his gaze drifted over her face; it was a strange sensation, as though he was reading something in her that she couldn’t feel or know about herself.
“You look tired,” he said finally, without moving his gaze away. “How long has it been since you slept?”
She blinked once, twice, trying to hide her surprise. She’d only been here for a minute; how did he know that she was tired at all? It couldn’t just be her imagination; there was something about the way his attention rested on her that made her feel suddenly very vulnerable, very exposed.

segment:
He tilted his head back again toward the padded wall, a wry smile curling his mouth. “What do you think?”
“I think maybe we should just stick to names,” she replied carefully.
He studied her intently for a second or two.
“Fair enough.”

Mara exhaled and sank into the chair, feeling a bit weary. She wondered how long she would have to wait here before someone else came along; if anyone ever did. The blond young man stayed on his couch, seeming content just to look at her. She tried not to feel uneasy as he studied her. It was like being a specimen in an exhibit for some kind of high school science fair.
“So you’re staying here?” she asked after what felt like an eternity of uncomfortable silence.
He grinned. “Yep.” He sounded oddly gleeful about it.
She frowned.
“Are you sure this is what you want to do with your life?” she asked cautiously, still feeling a bit wary of him.
